title: Speak SQL
subtitle: SELECT, FROM, and the shape of a result
description: SQL builds a result table from a source relation. Start by asking what one row represents.
bullets: SELECT chooses expressions and output columns; FROM determines the source rows.
PostgreSQL folds unquoted identifiers to lowercase. The lesson's orderNumber and ordernumber refer to the same unquoted identifier.
A projection can drop the key. DISTINCT removes duplicate output rows, not errors in your logic.
query: SELECT customernumber, customername, country\nFROM customers\nORDER BY customername;
concept: One row from customers is one customer. The primary key is customernumber.
sourceTopic: SQL, DDL, and DML · SELECT query · Basic SELECT queries

deepDive.title: A query is an ordered set of decisions
deepDive.question: What do SELECT, FROM, WHERE, and ORDER BY each contribute?
deepDive.resolution: FROM identifies source rows; WHERE chooses matching rows; SELECT constructs the output columns; ORDER BY arranges the returned result.
deepDive.sql:
SELECT customername, country
FROM customers
WHERE country = 'USA'
ORDER BY customername;

extra: The lecture also demonstrates computed columns with aliases, casts, and text predicates. Unquoted PostgreSQL column names are case-insensitive by default.

title: Filter & Sort
subtitle: WHERE, ORDER BY, FETCH FIRST
description: Filter individual source rows before aggregation. Sort only after the result is computed.
bullets: WHERE selects individual rows using predicates such as >, AND, IN and IS NULL.
ORDER BY specifies display order; SQL results have no guaranteed order without it.
FETCH FIRST limits the final result, while WITH TIES includes rows equal on every ORDER BY expression.
query:
SELECT ordernumber, orderdate
FROM orders
WHERE orderdate >= DATE '2024-01-01'
ORDER BY orderdate DESC;
concept: Think: FROM → WHERE → SELECT → ORDER BY → FETCH.

deepDive.title: The predicate changes rows; the sort changes their order
deepDive.question: Does ORDER BY filter away any rows?
deepDive.resolution: No. WHERE determines which rows survive; ORDER BY only rearranges the result. Use an explicit date range for a calendar-year filter.
deepDive.sql:
SELECT ordernumber, orderdate
FROM orders
WHERE orderdate >= DATE '2024-01-01'
  AND orderdate < DATE '2025-01-01'
ORDER BY orderdate;

extra: To inspect a future UPDATE/DELETE safely, use the same WHERE in a SELECT first.

title: CREATE & CRUD
subtitle: DDL versus DML; safe INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE
description: Build tables with DDL, then use DML to create, read, update, and delete rows. WHERE is the safety boundary for targeted changes.
bullets: CREATE TABLE defines column types, primary keys, and foreign key constraints.
INSERT creates rows; UPDATE changes matching rows; DELETE removes matching rows.
A missing WHERE on UPDATE or DELETE affects every row. Preview the predicate with SELECT first.
query:
SELECT customernumber, customername, creditlimit
FROM customers
WHERE creditlimit < 50000
ORDER BY customernumber;
concept: Before executing a destructive statement, run the same WHERE as a SELECT to verify exactly which rows it targets.
sourceTopic: SQL, DDL, and DML · Baby's First Query · INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE

deepDive.title: A safe CRUD experiment
deepDive.question: How can you try CREATE, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE without harming the practice dataset?
deepDive.resolution: Create a temporary table, insert one row, modify that row using WHERE, read it back, and delete it. This experiment uses a separate TEMP table.

extra: The free playground runs arbitrary SQL locally; use Restore data to recreate the original sample tables.

title: Build Joins
subtitle: INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN, and keys
description: Understand the identity of each intermediate joined row before projecting.
bullets: An order joined to its customer still produces one row per order.
An order joined to orderdetails produces one row per order line (ordernumber, productcode).
Joining two independent one-to-many children can multiply rows; LEFT JOIN keeps unmatched left rows.
query:
SELECT o.ordernumber, c.customername
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN customers c USING (customernumber)
ORDER BY o.ordernumber;
concept: Key question: what real-world thing does one joined row represent?
sourceTopic: The problem · Inner join variations · Multiple joins · Junction table joins

deepDive.title: USING versus ON
deepDive.question: What is the key after joining orders to customers?
deepDive.resolution: The ordernumber still identifies each joined row, because each order has one parent customer. ON permits differently named matching columns; USING merges an identically named join column in SELECT *.
deepDive.sql:
SELECT o.ordernumber, c.customername
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN customers c
  ON o.customernumber = c.customernumber
ORDER BY o.ordernumber;

extra: Joining orders → orderdetails → products follows the association path through a junction table; its key becomes (ordernumber, productcode).

title: Unmatched Rows
subtitle: LEFT JOIN, RIGHT JOIN, NULL and DISTINCT
description: INNER JOIN discards nonmatches; OUTER JOIN can retain rows even when no related record exists.
bullets: LEFT JOIN preserves every row on the left, setting unmatched right-table columns to NULL.
WHERE child.primarykey IS NULL finds parents with no children.
DISTINCT removes duplicate projected rows but cannot fix selecting the wrong set of rows.
query:
SELECT c.customernumber, c.customername
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o USING (customernumber)
WHERE o.ordernumber IS NULL
ORDER BY c.customernumber;
concept: A missing match is represented by NULLs, not by a special fake child row.
sourceTopic: Duplicate output · SELECT DISTINCT · Discarding unmatched rows · OUTER JOIN

deepDive.title: The missing-child pattern
deepDive.question: Why does INNER JOIN exclude customers who never ordered?
deepDive.resolution: No matching order means there is no joined row. A LEFT JOIN preserves the customer and produces NULL for order columns. Checking the child key IS NULL identifies these customers.
deepDive.sql:
SELECT c.customername
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o USING (customernumber)
WHERE o.ordernumber IS NULL
ORDER BY c.customername;

extra: LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL OUTER JOIN specify which unmatched source rows remain; NULL is the marker for the absent side.

title: Join Row Anatomy
subtitle: Keys, junction tables, and sibling joins
description: Joining two children through the same parent multiplies combinations. Analyze the intermediate key and row identity before aggregating.
bullets: orders JOIN orderdetails JOIN products keeps orderdetails' composite key (ordernumber, productcode).
orders JOIN customers JOIN payments pairs each order with each payment from the same customer; it does not mean the payment paid that order.
For one customer with 3 orders and 2 payments, the sibling join has 3 × 2 = 6 rows.
query:
SELECT o.ordernumber, p.checknumber, p.amount
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c USING (customernumber)
JOIN payments p USING (customernumber)
WHERE c.customernumber = 101
ORDER BY o.ordernumber, p.checknumber;
concept: The key of the sibling join combines ordernumber with the payment key; counting rows counts order–payment pairs, not orders or payments.
sourceTopic: Joined table schemas · Junction table joins · Joining to another child

deepDive.title: Orders × payments is not a receipt allocation
deepDive.question: A customer has two orders and two payments. Does their join have two rows?
deepDive.resolution: No. It has four order–payment combinations. You cannot infer which payment belongs to which order from shared customernumber alone.
deepDive.sql:
SELECT o.ordernumber, p.checknumber
FROM orders o
JOIN payments p USING(customernumber)
WHERE o.customernumber = 101
ORDER BY o.ordernumber, p.checknumber;

extra: The cardinality depends on the distribution of rows per customer, not just the table totals. A join's primary key may become a combination of child keys.

title: Count What Matters
subtitle: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX
description: Aggregate functions operate on input rows. A wrong join can silently inflate SUM or COUNT.
bullets: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values; COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts distinct non-NULL values.
SUM and AVG aggregate numeric expressions; MIN and MAX find extremes.
Check the join's key before trusting aggregate results.
query:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS number_of_orders,
       MIN(orderdate) AS first_order,
       MAX(orderdate) AS last_order
FROM orders;
concept: Joining 3 payments and 4 orders for one customer produces 12 rows, not 7.
sourceTopic: Aggregate functions · Selecting columns with an aggregate

deepDive.title: Count orders, not motorcycle line items
deepDive.question: If one order contains two motorcycle products, is COUNT(*) correct?
deepDive.resolution: No. The three-way join yields one row per matching orderdetail. COUNT(DISTINCT ordernumber) counts qualifying orders once.
deepDive.sql:
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT od.ordernumber) AS motorcycle_orders
FROM orders o
JOIN orderdetails od USING(ordernumber)
JOIN products p USING(productcode)
WHERE p.productline = 'Motorcycles';

extra: COUNT(*) counts matching rows, COUNT(column) ignores NULLs, and COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts different non-NULL values.

title: Groups & HAVING
subtitle: GROUP BY and group-level filters
description: GROUP BY changes one row's meaning from a detail record into an entire group.
bullets: If the goal says 'for each customer/year/country', look for GROUP BY.
WHERE filters input rows before grouping. HAVING filters completed groups.
Non-aggregated SELECT columns generally need to be in GROUP BY.
query:
SELECT c.country, COUNT(*) AS customer_count
FROM customers c
GROUP BY c.country
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY customer_count DESC, c.country;
concept: WHERE answers 'which individual rows?'; HAVING answers 'which groups?'.
sourceTopic: Grouping · Filtering based on aggregates · HAVING · Challenges

deepDive.title: A row total is not an order subtotal
deepDive.question: Why can't WHERE priceeach * quantityordered >= 1000 find orders worth at least 1000?
deepDive.resolution: WHERE tests one line item before grouping. HAVING tests the sum of all line items in an order after GROUP BY.
deepDive.sql:
SELECT ordernumber, SUM(priceeach * quantityordered) AS subtotal
FROM orderdetails
GROUP BY ordernumber
HAVING SUM(priceeach * quantityordered) >= 1000
ORDER BY ordernumber;

extra: Watch boundary words: 'at least' means >= rather than >. Also LEFT JOIN + COUNT(*) gives 1 for a customer with no orders; COUNT(ordernumber) gives 0.

title: One Value at a Time
subtitle: Scalar subqueries, unique keys, and ties
description: A scalar subquery stands in for one value. You must prove it returns at most one row, not merely observe that it does on today's data.
bullets: Using a full primary or unique key can ensure a subquery returns at most one row.
An aggregate with no GROUP BY produces one scalar row, including for empty input.
A query for MAX(amount) is scalar, but the rows having that amount may be many. Use IN/EXISTS or a join to preserve ties.
query:
SELECT DISTINCT c.customernumber, c.customername
FROM customers c
JOIN payments p USING (customernumber)
WHERE p.amount = (SELECT MAX(amount) FROM payments)
ORDER BY c.customernumber;
concept: The maximum value is one number. The payments attaining that number are not necessarily one row.
sourceTopic: Multi-question information needs · Scalar-value subqueries · Legal scalar subqueries

deepDive.title: Maximum payment, multiple winners
deepDive.question: Why might WHERE customernumber = (SELECT customernumber FROM payments WHERE amount = ...) fail?
deepDive.resolution: The inner MAX(amount) is one value, but multiple payments can match it. A subsequent customer lookup is a vector, so = can error. Join to payments and compare against the scalar MAX instead.
deepDive.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT c.customernumber, c.customername
FROM customers c JOIN payments p USING (customernumber)
WHERE p.amount = (SELECT MAX(amount) FROM payments)
ORDER BY c.customernumber;

extra: LIMIT/FETCH FIRST 1 ensures at most one row, but may discard legitimate ties; selecting a non-unique name cannot guarantee scalar cardinality.

title: Vector Subqueries
subtitle: IN, NOT IN, and the logic of exclusion
description: Vector-valued subqueries return a column of potentially many values. They are ideal for set membership and exclusion.
bullets: Use IN to keep outer rows whose key is in a one-column subquery result.
Use NOT IN or NOT EXISTS to keep rows outside the forbidden set, including those with no related child.
Finding a single instance that does not match a condition does not prove an entity never matched it.
query:
SELECT c.customernumber, c.customername
FROM customers c
WHERE c.customernumber NOT IN (
  SELECT o.customernumber FROM orders o
  WHERE o.orderdate >= DATE '2024-01-01'
    AND o.orderdate < DATE '2025-01-01'
)
ORDER BY c.customernumber;
concept: An exclusion condition often becomes easier by finding the disqualifying rows first.
sourceTopic: Vector-valued subqueries · NOT IN · January ordering counterexample

deepDive.title: One nonmatching order is not proof of never
deepDive.question: Can finding a customer's non-2024 order prove they placed no orders in 2024?
deepDive.resolution: No. That customer could also have a 2024 order. Collect customers who DID place a 2024 order and exclude that set with NOT IN (or NOT EXISTS).
deepDive.sql:
SELECT c.customernumber, c.customername
FROM customers c
WHERE c.customernumber NOT IN (
  SELECT o.customernumber FROM orders o
  WHERE o.orderdate >= DATE '2024-01-01'
    AND o.orderdate < DATE '2025-01-01'
)
ORDER BY c.customernumber;

extra: NOT IN is safe here because orders.customernumber is NOT NULL. If a subquery can return NULL, NOT EXISTS may be more reliable.

title: Derived Tables
subtitle: Subqueries in FROM and two-stage aggregates
description: A table subquery creates an intermediate relation with an explicit set of columns. The outer query can filter or aggregate those computed values.
bullets: A subquery in FROM requires an alias and exposes only the columns it selects.
To find average order subtotal, group line items into one row per order before AVG.
Counting customers by year requires COUNT(DISTINCT customernumber), not COUNT(*) of order rows.
concept: The intermediate derived table has its own schema and row meaning; only its selected columns exist for the outer query.
sourceTopic: Table-valued subqueries · markup · order years · average order subtotal

deepDive.title: Why aggregate twice?
deepDive.question: Why is AVG(quantityordered * priceeach) not average ORDER subtotal?
deepDive.resolution: The first averages orderdetail line totals. You must first SUM line totals per order, then AVG those per-order subtotals in the outer SELECT.

extra: Table subqueries are not magically materialized permanent tables. The outer SELECT sees only their projected columns and derived rows.

title: Debug the AI
subtitle: Diagnose plausible but incorrect SQL
description: Homework 8 asks you to reason about rows, keys, grouping, ties, and missing data without blindly executing SQL.
bullets: A correct-looking output shape does not prove you selected the correct rows.
DISTINCT fixes duplicated output rows, not multiplied SUM values or wrong predicates.
ORDER BY extra tie-breaker columns changes which rows qualify for WITH TIES.
query:
SELECT o.ordernumber
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN orderdetails od USING (ordernumber)
WHERE od.quantityordered > 50
ORDER BY o.ordernumber;
concept: Run the flawed query. Construct a counterexample. Repair the meaning—not just the formatting.
sourceTopic: Aggregate challenges · SELECT DISTINCT · Joining to another child · scalar/vector safety

deepDive.title: A correctly shaped answer can still be wrong
deepDive.question: Can a single row per customer prove SUM is correct?
deepDive.resolution: No. Grouping hides duplicated intermediate payment rows. Check the joined row key, remove unnecessary sibling joins, then sum the true payment rows.
deepDive.sql:
SELECT c.customernumber, c.customername, SUM(p.amount) AS total_payments
FROM customers c JOIN payments p USING(customernumber)
GROUP BY c.customernumber, c.customername
ORDER BY c.customername;

extra: Use the homework's counterexample habit: identify what one row means, what the key is, and find legal data where the AI query breaks.

title: Exam 3 Challenge
subtitle: Integrate every concept
description: Practice across joins, aggregates, HAVING, subqueries, and logical execution order.
bullets: Logical execution: FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → FETCH.
Inspect primary keys at every join and every subquery boundary.
Homework 8's five problem styles are reflected in the challenges. Use hints only after reasoning.
query:
SELECT c.customername, SUM(p.amount) AS total_payments
FROM customers c
JOIN payments p USING (customernumber)
GROUP BY c.customernumber, c.customername
ORDER BY total_payments DESC;
concept: Before writing code: identify required output columns, one-row meaning, and source table keys.
sourceTopic: SELECT · joins · aggregates · GROUP BY / HAVING · scalar/vector/table subqueries

deepDive.title: Solve in execution order
deepDive.question: Why does WHERE SUM(amount) > 100 fail?
deepDive.resolution: WHERE runs before GROUP BY and aggregates. Use HAVING after groups are formed, or compute the sum in a subquery and test the output in the outer WHERE.
deepDive.sql:
SELECT customernumber, SUM(amount) AS total_paid
FROM payments
GROUP BY customernumber
HAVING SUM(amount) > 1000
ORDER BY customernumber;

extra: Exam 3 focuses on the Homework database and the shape of joins, groups, and subqueries. Indexes and later topics are deliberately omitted.
